tagline.text: A grassy ridge trek in Subic, Zambales, where five peaks rise in a row

duration.label: Time needed
duration.text: 2 days 1 night (15–20 hours as a one-day traverse)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱1,500~3,500 (per person, rough estimate including transport from Manila and guide, based on a 2-day trip)

children.text: Cinco Picos means "five peaks" in Spanish, and the mountain, about 880 m high, rises in the Subic area at the southern end of the Zambales range. The appeal is a ridge climb over grass and rock, with camping above views of Subic Bay and Mount Balingkilat. A local Aeta guide is required.

Mount Cinco Picos rises behind Sitio Cawag in the municipality of Subic, Zambales. Its name is Spanish for "five peaks," and sure enough, large and small summits line up along the ridge. Sources give its height as anywhere from
to

, and its summit sits near 14.79° N, 120.16° E. The elevation is modest, but the trail starts almost at sea level, so the total ups and downs are large, and the long grassland ridge with little shade makes it feel tougher than the numbers suggest.

The area is the ancestral land of the Aeta people, and trail registration and guide assignment follow a system run by the village residents. A Philippine mountain-information site rates the standard 2-day course from Sitio Cawag at 3 out of 9 (major climb) and lists about
6.5 hours
to the summit. The Cawag Hexa traverse, which links six peaks in a single day, is rated 7, so the burden depends heavily on which route you choose, even on the same mountain.

The views are the biggest reward. On a clear day you can see Subic Bay and the coastline toward Olongapo to the east, and the South China Sea coast and the Balingkilat ridge to the west. From the camp near Peak 3 you can watch the sea of clouds at dusk and dawn and the stars at night, which has made it a word-of-mouth stargazing campsite not far from Manila.

Some things change often. Open sections, registration points and fees differ from year to year. Some recent accounts say only Peak 1 and the campsite near Peak 3 are open and the other peaks are restricted. Before you go, be sure to check the latest notice from the Subic tourism office or Sitio Cawag.
True to the name, peaks line up along the ridge, and the view changes with every climb. The standard route crosses Peaks 1 and 2 and camps below Peak 3, while Peaks 4 and 5 are seen from a distance.

blocks.title: Views of Subic Bay and Mount Balingkilat

children.text: From the ridge you can see the Subic Bay coast and Mount Balingkilat opposite. Visibility is best in the clear early morning, and clouds often roll in by the afternoon.

The campsite near Peak 3 has almost no light pollution, and on clear dry-season nights the Milky Way is visible. The wind picks up after sunset, so secure your tent well and bring plenty of warm clothing.
You hike with an Aeta guide from Sitio Cawag. A local who knows the trail goes with you, and the fees go back to the village, so your trip supports the community.

This course links six peaks in a day: Balingkilat, Bira-Bira, Naulaw, Dayungan, Cinco Picos and Redondo. Typical hikers take 15–20 hours and fast trail runners 8–13 hours, so it is a course for experienced hikers.

A route is known that descends the western slope of Cinco Picos, follows a river to Silanguin Cove, and takes a boat out to Anawangin or Pundaquit. The sources are old, however, so check locally whether it is currently open.
Most of the ridge is covered with tall grass and rock, so there is almost no shade. In return the views are open throughout the walk, and it is great for sunrise and sunset photos.

The dry season brings fewer clouds and good views from the ridge. December to February is recommended most often because the amihan (northeast monsoon) keeps it cool. The grassland ridge has almost no shade, so the risk of heat exhaustion rises sharply from March to May.

From June to September the habagat (southwest monsoon) brings frequent rain, strong ridge winds and typhoon risk. One weather record showed 19–24 rainy days a month from June to September. Rain makes the river rise and the rock sections slippery, so it is best to avoid this period.

blocks.label: Season at a glance
rows: The most recommended period. Mornings are cold, so bring warm clothing.
Watch for heat exhaustion and water shortage. Carry more water than usual.
Frequent rain, strong wind, possible typhoons
Avoid hiking. Check for trail restriction notices.
It may rain. Check the forecast before you go.

There is almost no lodging in the village below the mountain, so most people camp or make a day trip. On the 2-day course you pitch your tent at the campsite near Peak 3. It is safest to prepare camping gear in Manila beforehand.

You must handle meals yourself on the mountain, so bring simple food, energy bars and instant rice. After the hike you can find restaurants and convenience stores in Subic town. Accommodation is plentiful in Olongapo and on the Subic Bay side, and spending the night before in town gives you more time for early registration. Opening hours at the fire station and village hall can change, so check beforehand.

You can also spend the night before in Subic town or Olongapo and move out early in the morning. With a joiner van you leave Manila at night and reach the village around 1 a.m., which saves on lodging, but you start walking with almost no sleep. If you are not confident in your fitness, it is safer to choose the 2-day course and rest well in Subic the day before. After the hike, the usual routine is a hot meal and a shower in Subic town before taking a bus back to Manila.
A local guide is required. Solo hiking is prohibited, and one guide handles up to five hikers.
Carry 3–6 liters of water. Water points are few along the long route, so ration it carefully. Always purify stream water.
Early starts are the norm. Bring a headlamp of at least 1,000 lumens and spare batteries.
Long sleeves, long pants, a hat and sunscreen are needed. There is almost no shade, and tall grass easily scratches arms and legs.
Phone signal is unreliable and almost absent on the ridge. Download offline maps and stay with your guide.
Not recommended for beginners. Build fitness beforehand with walking and stair climbing.
A one-day Hexa traverse starts in the early hours and builds up sleepiness and fatigue. Know your early-exit points in advance.
Carry out all your trash, and respect the rules and culture of the indigenous village.
Check the last bus to Manila beforehand. A one-day traverse often ends late at night, so settle how you will get home first.

The long grassland ridge and rock sections with almost no shade carry a high risk of heat exhaustion and falls. Follow your guide's instructions and avoid hiking in the rainy season and during typhoons.
Open sections change over time. Some peaks are restricted, so check the latest notice.
Rain makes the river rise and the rock sections slippery. Postpone your trip if the forecast is bad.
Move one person at a time on the sharp parts of the Balingkilat ridge and on crumbly volcanic rock.
It is easy to get lost in tall grass, so do not leave the trail without your guide.
Fees and registration procedures change every year. Get a receipt and use official counters.
A quiet bay on the coast west of Cinco Picos, on the route by boat from Silanguin Cove. Boat service depends on the weather.
